1.modern-en: Lockwood visits his landlord at Wuthering Heights and congratulates himself on finding a fellow recluse. The dogs attack him when he is left alone; the reception is much less welcoming than he chooses to believe.

2.modern-en: A second visit leaves Lockwood trapped by snow. He repeatedly guesses the household’s relationships incorrectly, takes Joseph’s lantern to find his way home, and is knocked down by the dogs.

3.modern-en: In the enclosed bed, Lockwood reads Catherine’s scratched names and diary. He dreams of a sermon and then of a child at the window; his cries bring Heathcliff, whose distress surprises him.

4.modern-en: Back at the Grange, Lockwood asks Mrs. Dean about his neighbours. She corrects his understanding of the family and begins the history of Heathcliff’s arrival.

10.modern-en: Lockwood’s illness confines him to the Grange for weeks. During his recovery he resumes listening to Nelly’s account of the households.

14.modern-en: Lockwood responds to Nelly’s story by warning himself against attraction to the younger Catherine. He imagines the daughter repeating her mother’s history.

25.modern-en: Lockwood answers Nelly’s suggestions about an attachment to the younger Catherine but intends to leave. Her account brings the earlier history close to the time of his own visits.

30.modern-en: At the end of Nelly’s history, Lockwood resolves to leave for London. His recovered health makes another visit possible before he departs.

31.modern-en: Lockwood visits the Heights to announce his departure and carry Nelly’s note to Cathy. He witnesses the bitter exchanges between Cathy and Hareton and imagines himself as a possible romantic rescuer.

32.modern-en: Returning in September 1802, Lockwood learns that Nelly has moved to the Heights. There he sees Cathy helping Hareton read and hears that Heathcliff is dead.

34.modern-en: After hearing the end of the history, Lockwood visits the graves of Catherine, Edgar and Heathcliff. The quiet landscape prompts his final reflection on their rest.

4.modern-en: Nelly identifies the young widow as Catherine Linton and recalls growing up with the Earnshaws. She admits her own cruelty to Heathcliff when Mr. Earnshaw first brings him home.

7.modern-en: Nelly encourages Heathcliff to wash and dress himself and tries to counter his shame about his appearance. Her account pauses for a conversation with Lockwood about education and storytelling.

9.modern-en: Nelly questions Catherine about her decision to marry Edgar and notices Heathcliff leave during the conversation. She later accompanies Catherine to the Grange, reluctantly leaving Hareton behind.

11.modern-en: Nelly visits the Heights and discovers Hareton’s hostility and ignorance. Back at the Grange she reports Heathcliff’s conduct toward Isabella, helping precipitate a confrontation with Edgar.

12.modern-en: Nelly initially treats Catherine’s refusal to eat as wilfulness. Recognising the seriousness of her illness, she brings Edgar and seeks medical help.

14.modern-en: Nelly visits Isabella but cannot bring the reconciliation with Edgar that she wants. Heathcliff presses Nelly into carrying a letter to Catherine and arranging access to her.

15.modern-en: Nelly delivers Heathcliff’s letter and admits him while Edgar is at church. She struggles to end the visit before Edgar returns and then tries to manage the crisis.

16.modern-en: Nelly tells Heathcliff of Catherine’s death and witnesses his violent grief. She notices the changed contents of Catherine’s locket and describes the funeral and burial.

17.modern-en: Nelly receives the fleeing Isabella and hears her account. She later discovers the extent of Hindley’s debts and the consequences for Hareton.

18.modern-en: Nelly searches for the missing Cathy and finds her at the Heights. She persuades her to conceal the visit from Edgar, partly to protect her own position.

20.modern-en: Nelly takes Linton to the Heights under Edgar’s instructions. She tries to soften the journey for the frightened boy but must leave him pleading to return with her.

21.modern-en: Nelly objects to the visit and later discovers Cathy’s letters. She makes Cathy burn them and sends Linton a message ending the correspondence.

22.modern-en: Nelly resists Heathcliff’s appeal and then reluctantly accompanies Cathy to the Heights. She hopes Linton’s reception will disprove the story that has upset her.

23.modern-en: The wet journey leaves Nelly ill and confined to her room. She mistakes Cathy’s flushed cheeks after evening visits for the effect of sitting beside the library fire.

24.modern-en: Recovered enough to leave her room, Nelly discovers Cathy’s absences and hears her confession. She tells Edgar despite Cathy’s expectation of confidence.

25.modern-en: Nelly locates these events only a little more than a year before her conversation with Lockwood. She recalls Edgar’s illness and her mistaken hope that Linton was recovering.

26.modern-en: Nelly accompanies Cathy and observes Linton’s alarming condition. She cannot decide how much of their disturbing encounter to tell Edgar.

27.modern-en: Nelly accompanies Cathy into the Heights and is imprisoned separately. For several days she sees only Hareton, who brings food but does not help her leave.

28.modern-en: Zillah releases Nelly, who hurries to the dying Edgar and seeks help for Cathy. Cathy escapes in time to reach her father before his death.

29.modern-en: Nelly asks to remain with Cathy but is refused. She hears Heathcliff’s account of the grave and watches him take her former charge away.

32.modern-en: Nelly welcomes Lockwood and recounts the change since she joined Cathy at the Heights. She describes the gradual reconciliation between Cathy and Hareton and hopes for their marriage.

34.modern-en: Nelly observes Heathcliff’s final days and finds his body. She reports the local stories about his ghost without establishing their truth, and describes the young couple’s plans.

1.modern-en: Heathcliff reluctantly admits his new tenant, orders Joseph to take the horse and leaves Lockwood among the dogs. He eventually talks with him, without encouraging another visit.

2.modern-en: Heathcliff corrects Lockwood’s assumptions about the young woman and Hareton. He gives little help when the visitor cannot leave, but eventually allows him to stay overnight.

3.modern-en: Heathcliff is angry to find Lockwood in the bedroom. After hearing about the dream, he opens the window and begs Catherine to come in, revealing grief the visitor cannot explain.

4.modern-en: Mr. Earnshaw brings the homeless child from Liverpool and the household names him Heathcliff. He becomes close to Cathy, suffers Hindley’s abuse and uses Mr. Earnshaw’s favour to obtain Hindley’s horse.

5.modern-en: Mr. Earnshaw’s favour protects Heathcliff but intensifies Hindley’s resentment. After the old man’s death, Heathcliff and Catherine comfort one another with their thoughts of heaven.

6.modern-en: Heathcliff and Catherine spy through the Grange window. When the Lintons’ dog bites Catherine, she is taken inside while he is treated as a criminal and sent away.

7.modern-en: Heathcliff asks Nelly to help make him presentable for the Lintons’ visit. Edgar’s remark about his hair provokes him to throw hot applesauce; Hindley punishes him, and he broods on revenge.

8.modern-en: Heathcliff resents Catherine’s time with Edgar and tries to count the attention she gives each of them. His neglected education and lowered household position make the rivalry increasingly painful.

9.modern-en: Heathcliff catches Hareton when the child falls from Hindley’s arms. Later he overhears Catherine say that marrying him would degrade her and leaves before hearing the rest of her explanation.

10.modern-en: Heathcliff returns after a long absence, changed in appearance and manner. Catherine welcomes him enthusiastically; he lodges with Hindley and takes an interest in Isabella’s attraction to him.

11.modern-en: Heathcliff embraces Isabella and declares his purpose of revenge to Catherine. His confrontation with Edgar exposes the violence beneath their attempts at social restraint.

13.modern-en: Isabella’s letter describes Heathcliff’s conduct as a husband and his hostility toward the households around him. He offers her none of the protection she expected from marriage.

14.modern-en: Heathcliff insists on seeing Catherine despite Nelly’s warnings about her health. He forces a promise of help by threatening to make his own way into the Grange.

15.modern-en: Heathcliff visits the ill Catherine with Nelly’s assistance. He accuses her of having destroyed their lives, holds her when she collapses and leaves only after Edgar takes over her care.

16.modern-en: Heathcliff receives news of Catherine’s death and begs her to haunt him rather than leave him alone. He visits her body and alters the keepsake in her locket.

17.modern-en: Heathcliff fights Hindley and attacks Isabella before her escape. After Hindley’s death he takes possession of the mortgaged estate and keeps Hareton dependent on him.

20.modern-en: Heathcliff scrutinises and mocks his son’s frailty while explaining his ambitions for him. He prevents the boy from following Nelly back to the Grange.

21.modern-en: Heathcliff draws Cathy into a visit and explains his hopes for a marriage between her and Linton. His account of Hareton’s upbringing makes education part of his revenge.

22.modern-en: Heathcliff blames Cathy for Linton’s supposed decline and urges her to see him while he himself is away. Nelly distrusts his account but cannot quiet Cathy’s distress.

27.modern-en: Heathcliff draws Cathy and Nelly into Wuthering Heights and locks them in. He uses violence and confinement to force a marriage before Edgar dies.

29.modern-en: Heathcliff takes Cathy back to the Heights after Edgar’s funeral. He tells Nelly of disturbing Catherine’s grave and of the presence he believes has haunted him since her death.

30.modern-en: Heathcliff secures control after Linton’s death and keeps Cathy isolated at the Heights. Nelly cannot obtain permission to bring her back to the Grange.

31.modern-en: Heathcliff hears Lockwood’s intention to leave and remarks on Hareton’s resemblance to Catherine. Lockwood observes his preoccupation and the household’s hostility.

33.modern-en: Seeing Cathy and Hareton together, Heathcliff finds reminders of the elder Catherine that weaken his desire to complete his revenge. He tells Nelly that an approaching change absorbs his attention.

34.modern-en: Heathcliff stops eating regularly, wanders at night and appears absorbed by something the others cannot see. Nelly finds him dead beside the open window and arranges his burial according to his wishes.

epithet.en: A name in the old bedroom

3.modern-en: Catherine’s names and old diary occupy the bedroom where Lockwood sleeps. The diary describes rebellion against Hindley and Joseph; the child in Lockwood’s dream calls herself Catherine Linton.

4.modern-en: As a small child, Cathy asks her father for a whip and resents the loss of her present when he brings home Heathcliff instead. Nelly then recalls the children becoming close companions.

5.modern-en: Catherine tests her father’s patience but seeks his affection. On the evening of his death she is beside his chair; afterwards she and Heathcliff console each other.

6.modern-en: Catherine shares lessons and outdoor adventures with Heathcliff despite Hindley’s restrictions. A dog bites her ankle at the Grange, where recognition of her family wins her admission.

7.modern-en: Catherine returns after five weeks at the Grange, dressed and behaving like a young lady. Her laughter at Heathcliff’s appearance hurts him, though she wants to renew their companionship.

8.modern-en: Catherine keeps up her friendship with Edgar while growing impatient with Heathcliff. During Edgar’s visit she strikes Nelly and then Edgar, but his attempted departure ends in reconciliation.

9.modern-en: Catherine tells Nelly she has accepted Edgar but describes her attachment to Heathcliff as inseparable from herself. After Heathcliff disappears she searches for him, becomes ill and eventually marries Edgar.

10.modern-en: Catherine rejoices at Heathcliff’s return and demands that Edgar welcome him. When Isabella confides her attraction, Catherine warns her against him but also exposes her feelings in his presence.

11.modern-en: Catherine provokes the confrontation between Edgar and Heathcliff and refuses the choice Edgar demands. She retreats to her room and threatens to make herself ill.

12.modern-en: After refusing food, Catherine becomes delirious and longs for the childhood home she imagines around her. She scarcely recognises herself in the mirror and wants the window opened onto the moors.

13.modern-en: Catherine survives the worst of her fever but remains fragile. Edgar nurses her closely, hoping for a recovery that Kenneth regards much less confidently.

15.modern-en: Catherine receives Heathcliff during Edgar’s absence. Their reunion becomes an exchange of accusations and desperate embraces; she collapses as Edgar returns.

16.modern-en: Catherine dies two hours after giving birth, without recovering consciousness. Nelly describes her stillness and the unusual position of her grave at the edge of the churchyard.

epithet.en: The young woman at the Heights

2.modern-en: The young Mrs. Heathcliff receives Lockwood coldly and quarrels with Joseph. Heathcliff identifies her as his daughter-in-law and his son’s widow, correcting the visitor’s guesses.

4.modern-en: Nelly identifies the young Mrs. Heathcliff as her former charge, Catherine Linton, and distinguishes her from the Catherine associated with Lockwood’s bedroom experience.

16.modern-en: The younger Catherine is born prematurely during the night. Nelly recounts the neglect surrounding her first hours as the household is overwhelmed by her mother’s death.

18.modern-en: Cathy grows up at the Grange under Edgar’s care and teaching. While he is away, she sets out toward Penistone Crags and meets Hareton, whom she mistakes for a servant.

19.modern-en: Cathy eagerly welcomes the cousin she has imagined and takes pleasure in looking after him. She does not know that Heathcliff is demanding his removal.

21.modern-en: On her sixteenth birthday, Cathy encounters Heathcliff and visits the Heights with Nelly. She renews acquaintance with Linton and later exchanges secret letters with him until Nelly discovers them.

22.modern-en: With Edgar ill, Cathy worries about losing him. Heathcliff meets her outside the park and claims Linton is suffering from her neglect, persuading her to seek another visit.

23.modern-en: Cathy quarrels with Linton and then feels responsible for his suffering. After Nelly becomes ill, she begins riding secretly to the Heights in the evenings.

24.modern-en: Cathy confesses her secret visits to Nelly. She recounts quarrels with Linton and her treatment of Hareton; after Nelly tells Edgar, further visits are forbidden.

26.modern-en: Cathy meets Linton on the moors and is disappointed by his weakness and indifference. His fear at the thought of another meeting leaves her uneasy rather than reassured.

27.modern-en: Cathy begs to return to her dying father, resists Heathcliff and tries to obtain the key. He confines her until she agrees to marry Linton.

28.modern-en: Now married to Linton, Cathy secures his help to escape through a window. She returns to Edgar and comforts him in his final hours.

29.modern-en: Cathy resists Heathcliff’s contempt and insists that she and Linton can still care for one another. She must leave Nelly and the Grange to live at the Heights.

30.modern-en: Cathy nurses Linton without the help she seeks from the household. After his death she withdraws from the others, responding to their neglect with hostility.

31.modern-en: Cathy receives Nelly’s note but mocks Hareton’s attempts to read. Her anger over the loss of her books helps turn his interest in learning into another occasion for humiliation.

32.modern-en: Cathy apologises to Hareton and offers him a book as a peace offering. Their friendship grows through reading together and a willingness to repair earlier injuries.

33.modern-en: Cathy persuades Hareton to clear part of Joseph’s garden for flowers. When Heathcliff confronts them, she speaks against his treatment of them and finds that Hareton will still defend him.

34.modern-en: Cathy and Hareton plan their marriage and life at the Grange. Their companionship gives the two households a future different from the quarrels Nelly has recounted.

3.modern-en: In Catherine’s childhood diary, Hindley insists on obedience and mistreats Heathcliff. Catherine compares his rule unfavourably with her father’s.

4.modern-en: Hindley resents the child his father has brought home and the favour shown to him. Their dispute over the horses brings his violent treatment of Heathcliff into the open.

5.modern-en: Hindley is sent to college on the curate’s advice. His absence briefly reduces the conflict over Mr. Earnshaw’s preference for Heathcliff.

6.modern-en: Hindley returns for his father’s funeral with a wife and takes control of Wuthering Heights. He stops Heathcliff’s education and puts him to work outside with the servants.

7.modern-en: Hindley excludes Heathcliff from the company and punishes him after the incident with Edgar. The festive household gives Heathcliff further reasons to resent his treatment.

8.modern-en: Frances’s death drives Hindley into reckless drinking and violent behaviour. Nelly hides Hareton and unloads his father’s gun to reduce the danger.

9.modern-en: Drunk and violent, Hindley threatens Nelly and endangers Hareton. The household’s disorder continues while Catherine makes plans to leave it through marriage.

10.modern-en: Hindley invites Heathcliff to stay at Wuthering Heights. Reports of their gambling and drinking trouble Nelly, who fears further ruin for the household.

13.modern-en: Hindley shows Isabella the weapon with which he plans to attack Heathcliff. Her arrival exposes the violence and disorder of life at the Heights.

17.modern-en: Isabella recounts Hindley’s failed attack on Heathcliff. Later Hindley dies, leaving debts that allow Heathcliff to establish control of Wuthering Heights.

epithet.en: The young man at the Heights

2.modern-en: The young man at the table angrily identifies himself as Hareton Earnshaw after Lockwood mistakes his relationship to Mrs. Heathcliff. His name does not explain his position in the house.

4.modern-en: Nelly identifies Hareton as Hindley’s son. She tells Lockwood that he has been wronged without understanding what has been taken from him.

8.modern-en: Hareton is born during haymaking. After Frances dies, Nelly becomes his principal carer while Hindley sinks into grief and drinking.

9.modern-en: Hareton is endangered by his drunken father and caught by Heathcliff when he falls. Later he loses Nelly’s daily care when she moves to the Grange with Catherine.

11.modern-en: Hareton meets Nelly with stones and curses. He says Heathcliff has taught him to swear at his father and that the curate no longer teaches him.

13.modern-en: Isabella encounters Hareton in the neglected household and struggles to obtain help or civility. Her letter shows how far his upbringing differs from life at the Grange.

17.modern-en: After Hindley’s death, Hareton remains at Wuthering Heights under Heathcliff’s control. He has lost his expected position without understanding how the property passed from his father.

18.modern-en: Hareton accompanies Cathy on her excursion and shows her local sights. Their initial friendliness collapses when she treats him as a servant and resists the news that they are cousins.

21.modern-en: Cathy and Linton ridicule Hareton’s inability to read the name above the door. Heathcliff describes to Nelly how he has kept the young man ignorant and dependent.

24.modern-en: Hareton tries to show Cathy his newly acquired reading ability and receives ridicule. His hurt and anger disrupt the company she seeks with Linton.

27.modern-en: Hareton acts as Nelly’s jailer, bringing food during her confinement. He refuses her appeals for release.

31.modern-en: Hareton’s concealed efforts to learn are exposed to Cathy’s ridicule. He throws his books into the fire in anger and shame.

32.modern-en: Hareton is slow to trust Cathy’s approach after her mockery. He accepts the offered friendship and returns to learning with her help.

33.modern-en: Hareton helps Cathy alter the garden but refuses to join her attacks on Heathcliff. His attachment to the man who raised him complicates his new alliance with her.

34.modern-en: Hareton mourns Heathcliff sincerely and cares for his body. He and Cathy plan to marry and move to the Grange.

6.modern-en: Heathcliff describes Edgar quarrelling with Isabella over a little dog in their comfortable drawing room. Edgar recognises the injured Catherine as Miss Earnshaw.

7.modern-en: Edgar comes to the Heights at Christmas with Isabella. His comment about Heathcliff’s hair leads to an outburst that interrupts the visit.

8.modern-en: Edgar sees Catherine strike Nelly and then is struck himself. He tries to leave, but her distress draws him back and their intimacy deepens.

9.modern-en: Edgar marries Catherine three years after his father’s death and brings her to the Grange. Nelly goes with her despite her attachment to Hareton.

10.modern-en: Edgar reluctantly admits Heathcliff as a visitor for Catherine’s sake. He is troubled by the renewed intimacy and the effect of Heathcliff’s presence on his household.

11.modern-en: Edgar orders Heathcliff from the house and tells Catherine she must choose between them. He warns Isabella that encouraging Heathcliff would break her family ties.

12.modern-en: Edgar discovers how ill Catherine has become and turns to caring for her. When Isabella’s flight with Heathcliff is reported, he says she has separated herself from the family.

13.modern-en: Edgar devotes himself to Catherine’s recovery. He does not reply to Isabella’s announcement that she has married Heathcliff.

15.modern-en: Edgar returns from church to find Catherine unconscious in Heathcliff’s arms. His alarm for her takes precedence over the confrontation he might otherwise have begun.

16.modern-en: Edgar is devastated by Catherine’s death. His grief leaves the newborn child temporarily without the attention Nelly believes she needs.

18.modern-en: Edgar educates his daughter and limits her knowledge of the neighbouring household. He leaves to visit the dying Isabella, creating the opportunity for Cathy’s unsupervised adventure.

19.modern-en: After Isabella’s death, Edgar returns with her son Linton. He hopes to care for the boy, but Joseph arrives to demand him on Heathcliff’s behalf.

22.modern-en: Edgar’s cold settles on his lungs and confines him indoors. His daughter’s fear for him leaves her particularly vulnerable to Heathcliff’s claims about Linton.

24.modern-en: Edgar forbids Cathy’s visits to the Heights after Nelly reports them. He offers instead to invite Linton to the Grange, without knowing the boy’s true condition.

25.modern-en: Edgar considers the possibility of his daughter marrying Linton and worries about her future. Linton’s letters encourage hopes that his actual health and circumstances cannot support.

28.modern-en: Edgar waits for his daughter as he is dying. Cathy reaches him in time, and he dies believing that she can be happy.

6.modern-en: Isabella quarrels with Edgar over the dog and then recoils from Heathcliff when the captured children are brought inside. The scene is reported through Heathcliff’s hostile account.

7.modern-en: Isabella visits the Heights with Edgar for Christmas. Heathcliff’s outburst disrupts the gathering, exposing the hostility beneath its polite arrangements.

10.modern-en: Isabella becomes attracted to Heathcliff and confides in Catherine. Catherine’s warning turns into a humiliating disclosure before him, leaving Isabella angry and exposed.

11.modern-en: Isabella’s involvement with Heathcliff brings a warning from Edgar. She evades her brother’s questions rather than offering the rejection of Heathcliff he wants.

12.modern-en: Isabella leaves with Heathcliff. The news reaches the Grange while Catherine is seriously ill, and Edgar refuses further inquiry into his sister’s choice.

13.modern-en: Isabella writes to Nelly after her marriage, describing an inhospitable arrival at the Heights, Hindley’s threats and Heathcliff’s cruelty. She asks Nelly to come rather than merely write.

14.modern-en: Isabella asks Nelly about Edgar and receives no invitation to return. Heathcliff speaks contemptuously about her in Nelly’s presence, exposing the misery of the marriage.

17.modern-en: Isabella escapes from the Heights after a violent encounter involving Heathcliff and Hindley. She leaves the neighbourhood, settles near London and later gives birth to a son named Linton.

epithet.en: The child named in Isabella’s letters

17.modern-en: Nelly first names Isabella’s son, born after her escape and described in her letters as sickly and fretful. Heathcliff learns of his existence through other servants.

19.modern-en: Linton arrives at the Grange after his mother’s death, tired and frail. Cathy welcomes him eagerly, but his father’s claim interrupts the prospect of remaining with Edgar.

20.modern-en: Linton discovers that he is being taken to a father he does not know. Heathcliff’s reception frightens him, and he begs Nelly not to leave him there.

21.modern-en: Linton receives Cathy at the Heights and joins in mocking Hareton’s lack of education. Their renewed acquaintance develops into a correspondence that Nelly interrupts.

23.modern-en: Linton reproaches Cathy and demands her attention during the visit. Their quarrel and his coughing distress her, and she tries to comfort him before leaving.

24.modern-en: Cathy’s account reveals Linton’s demands, sulking and fear of his father. Their visits offer little of the happy companionship she had imagined.

25.modern-en: Linton’s letters press for meetings with Cathy. Nelly explains that Heathcliff’s pressure, rather than improving health, lies behind the boy’s apparent eagerness.

26.modern-en: Linton is too weak to reach the agreed meeting place. His anxiety about his father and dependence on Cathy’s promises reveal how little freedom he has.

27.modern-en: Terrified of Heathcliff, Linton helps lure Cathy and Nelly into the house. His fear of punishment outweighs his ability to protect Cathy from his father’s demands.

28.modern-en: Linton boasts to Nelly about his rights over Cathy’s belongings and repeats his father’s cruel claims. He later helps Cathy escape, exposing himself to Heathcliff’s punishment.

30.modern-en: Zillah’s account describes Linton’s final illness and death. The arrangements made under Heathcliff’s pressure leave Cathy without control of the property she expected.

1.modern-en: Joseph receives orders to attend to Lockwood’s horse and then to bring wine. Lockwood finds his manner sour and his religious exclamations unwelcoming.

2.modern-en: Joseph refuses to guide Lockwood through the snow and protests when he takes the lantern. The resulting alarm brings the dogs upon the departing visitor.

3.modern-en: The diary recalls Joseph enforcing religious exercises and punishing the children. In the morning he again quarrels with the young Mrs. Heathcliff.

5.modern-en: Joseph gains influence over the declining Mr. Earnshaw through religious rebukes and complaints about the children. After the death he helps arrange the household’s response.

13.modern-en: In Isabella’s account, Joseph offers little help to the new bride and quarrels over domestic arrangements. His behaviour helps make her first evening at the Heights miserable.

19.modern-en: Joseph arrives at the Grange to insist that Heathcliff’s son be sent to him. Edgar postpones the transfer until morning despite Joseph’s anger.

33.modern-en: Joseph protests when his currant and gooseberry bushes are removed. His complaint brings the younger pair’s cooperation to Heathcliff’s attention.

3.modern-en: Catherine’s diary describes Frances pulling Heathcliff’s hair at Hindley’s request and then sitting on her husband’s knee while the children shelter behind a makeshift curtain.

6.modern-en: Hindley brings Frances home as his wife, without explaining her background. She first fusses over Catherine and then helps plan to separate her from Heathcliff’s influence.

8.modern-en: Frances gives birth to Hareton and soon dies after an illness. Hindley refuses to accept Kenneth’s warning that she will not recover.

4.modern-en: Mr. Earnshaw walks to Liverpool and returns with a starving child whose family he cannot discover. His growing affection for Heathcliff deepens the hostility within his own household.

5.modern-en: As his health fails, Mr. Earnshaw becomes increasingly irritable and protective of Heathcliff. He dies quietly by the fire, with Catherine beside him.

4.modern-en: Mrs. Earnshaw waits anxiously for her husband’s return and angrily resists keeping the unknown child. Nelly recalls her failure to defend Heathcliff from mistreatment and her death within two years.

6.modern-en: Mr. Linton assumes the unknown boy is connected with robbers. He recognises Catherine’s position, criticises Hindley’s neglect and subsequently visits the Heights to rebuke him.

9.modern-en: Nelly recalls that Mr. Linton and his wife both catch the fever after Mrs. Linton takes the recovering Catherine to the Grange. They die within a few days of one another.

6.modern-en: Mrs. Linton reacts with horror to Heathcliff and to Catherine’s appearance in his company. The family treats the injured Catherine as a child entitled to their care.

9.modern-en: Mrs. Linton visits the ill Catherine, takes charge of her care and brings her to the Grange during her recovery. She and her husband catch the fever and die.

8.modern-en: Kenneth warns that Frances is seriously ill. Hindley angrily rejects his judgment and insists that she will be well again shortly.

2.modern-en: Zillah intervenes after the dogs knock Lockwood down. She helps revive him and takes him upstairs for the night.

3.modern-en: Zillah gives Lockwood a room that Heathcliff usually keeps closed. She warns him to be quiet and admits that she does not understand the household’s strange arrangements.

28.modern-en: Returning to the Heights, Zillah opens Nelly’s room. She has accepted Heathcliff’s explanation of the women’s disappearance and does not initially understand the imprisonment.

30.modern-en: Zillah supplies Nelly with news from the Heights. Her resentment of Cathy’s manner colours an account in which the young woman receives little assistance during Linton’s illness.

6.modern-en: Mr. Linton names the curate Shielders as the source of complaints about Hindley’s neglect of Catherine’s upbringing.
